title: Interface as Contract
story: Remember contracts from L4? `requires` and `ensures` on functions? Interfaces are contracts at the TYPE level. When you write `fn compute[T: Multipliable](a: T, b: T) -> T`, you're saying 'I contractually guarantee that T has a multiply method.' The compiler is your notary — it verifies every type passed to this function keeps the contract.
why: Interfaces are compile-time contracts — they guarantee specific methods exist on a type, just like `requires` guarantees input conditions and `ensures` guarantees output conditions.
analogy: An interface contract is like a rental car agreement — the contract says 'this car has brakes, steering, and an engine.' You don't check each time you drive; the contract (compiler) guarantees it. If the car were missing a steering wheel, the contract wouldn't have been signed (the code wouldn't compile).
try_it: Implement Addable for a `Money` type with `dollars: Int` and `cents: Int`. Make `add` handle cent overflow (100 cents = 1 dollar). Then write a function with TWO constraints: `[T: Addable + Displayable]` — the function sums items AND prints the running total. What happens if you call this function with Meter (which has Addable) — does Meter need Displayable to compile?
tips: `[T: Greetable]` is a type-level contract — the compiler enforces it just like `requires:` enforces value contracts
`Self` in interfaces refers to the implementing type — `fn add(other: &Self) -> Self` means 'takes same type, returns same type'
Multiple interface constraints (`+`) work like multiple requires clauses — all must be satisfied
common_mistakes: Confusing value contracts (requires/ensures) with type contracts (interfaces) — they work at different levels
Writing `fn is_equal(other: T) -> Bool` without `&` — `Self` in interfaces should use `&Self` for borrowing
Assuming interface methods can have contracts — some XIOM versions may support `requires` inside interfaces for even stronger guarantees
